entries.name: Curtis Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses AI/ML, computational modeling, high-throughput molecular profiling and experiments to study how tumours evolve, with the aim of improving cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment. Current projects include early cancer evolution (for example Barrett's esophagus and intestinal metaplasia, using organoid models and multiomic profiling) and tissue ecology in ER+ breast cancer. A large part of the work is single-cell and spatial transcriptomics and spatial multiomics, including how cancer cells and the microenvironment coevolve. The lab also does computational pathology and builds prognostic biomarkers from genomic and imaging data. Evolutionary and mathematical modelling of tumour growth is also part of the group's approach.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with cancer genomics, computational/ML methods and single-cell and spatial omics in cancer. Less emphasis on WGS and structural-variant calling, and a US move would need a visa.

entries.name: Goodarzi Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds AI/ML models for functional genomics. These include interpretable neural networks of DNA and RNA regulation, and large language and foundation models for chemistry and genomics. It studies cancer evolution and tumour-environment interactions, including how cancer cells reprogram gene expression. A central example is orphan non-coding RNAs (oncRNAs), which are largely absent from normal tissue and promote metastasis. It also studies post-transcriptional regulation in cancer and neurodegeneration, for example tRNA fragments (tiRNAs) that suppress breast cancer metastasis. Its methods pair unbiased experimental screens with computational analysis.

fit.reason: Strong overlap on computational and ML methods for genomics and on cancer transcriptomics, but the lab centres on RNA biology and model building rather than tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation analysis, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Alexandrov Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops machine-learning and computational approaches to study the molecular mechanisms of cancer development and progression. Its core theme is mutational signatures: it develops the SigProfiler software suite and works with the Wellcome Sanger Institute on the COSMIC signature catalogue. Work includes applying signature methods to copy-number and structural variants in cancer genomes, APOBEC mutagenesis, and clonal hematopoiesis. It also uses duplex and other highly accurate sequencing of normal tissues to study how environmental exposures, ageing, and DNA repair leave mutational footprints. Alexandrov leads the Cancer Grand Challenges CAUSE team on the mechanisms behind mutational signatures. The lab is recruiting postdocs for pre-cancer evolution and for experimental DNA damage/repair work.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with somatic mutation and structural variant analysis, cancer WGS, and computational/ML methods. There is little single-cell or spatial omics and no emphasis on transcriptome work, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Getz Lab
entries.focus: The lab does cancer genome analysis in two steps. Characterization catalogs genomic events and their causes in an individual patient's tumour compared with normal tissue, across DNA, RNA and protein. Interpretation analyses these data across patient cohorts to find cancer-driving gene and pathway alterations, molecular subtypes, and links to clinical variables. Current themes listed on the PI's Broad bio are tumour heterogeneity and clonal evolution, single-cell analysis of tumours and the microenvironment, therapy-resistance drivers, proteogenomics, and somatic mutations in normal tissues. The group also leads the Broad effort in the TCGA Genome Data Analysis Center and co-leads the Proteogenomics Data Analysis Center.

fit.reason: The lab is a leading computational cancer-genomics group working on WGS/transcriptome somatic analysis, mutation and driver methods, and single-cell tumour profiling. This closely matches the student's interests, though US visa logistics and a large lab are drawbacks.

entries.name: Ideker Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds network and hierarchical models of the cell, such as the Cancer Cell Map Initiative, and uses them to interpret genetic variation and disease. The lab develops the Cytoscape network analysis software, and its work spans cancer genomics, protein interaction mapping, and machine learning.

entries.name: Palotie Lab
entries.focus: The group studies the genetic mechanisms of common diseases using clinical and population samples from the Finnish founder population. The main emphasis is on neurological, neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric traits, especially migraine, schizophrenia and epilepsy, their comorbidities, and some cardiovascular traits. Methods include large genome-wide association and sequencing studies, and family-based designs that exploit population bottlenecks to find low-frequency variants. Palotie is also Scientific Director of the FinnGen biobank project, which links genomes and health records for about 500,000 Finnish participants.

fit.reason: The lab works on germline population genetics of brain disorders, with no evident cancer, tumour sequencing, somatic or structural-variant, or single-cell/spatial work; the only overlap is general computational genomics.

entries.name: Nirmal Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how the tumour microenvironment changes as melanoma progresses from normal skin through precursor and in situ lesions to invasive disease. It also studies how a tumour cell's position relative to immune cells shapes its molecular state and drug response. Methods include multiplexed imaging (CyCIF), spatial transcriptomics, scRNA-seq, micro-region sequencing, and 3D tissue reconstruction. The computational side covers machine learning and statistics: the SCIMAP spatial single-cell Python toolkit, the GATOR deep-learning phenotyping framework, a spatial-lag algorithm, and an LDA-based model of recurrent cellular neighbourhoods.

fit.reason: The lab matches the student's interest in computational methods and ML for single-cell and spatial omics in cancer, but it centres on imaging-based spatial proteomics in melanoma, with little tumour WGS or structural-variant work. A US role would also need a visa.

entries.name: Gusev Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops computational and statistical methods to understand the heritable (germline) component of cancer and other common diseases from large-scale data. It integrates molecular data to interpret genome-wide association study findings and helped develop the transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS) approach for mapping disease-linked genes. A second theme is precision oncology: how germline and somatic tumour alterations interact to shape cancer progression and treatment response. Recent work includes machine-learning prediction of a tumour's primary site from clinical sequencing data (OncoNPC) and LLM-based analysis of patient records in immunotherapy.

fit.reason: Overlaps with the student's cancer genomics and computational/ML methods interests, but the lab leans toward germline statistical genetics and clinical-data modelling rather than tumour WGS/SV analysis or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Villani Lab
entries.focus: The lab builds a detailed map of the human immune system, covering the cell types involved and the rules that govern immune responses. It uses single-cell multi-omics, systems immunology and computational modelling to study immunity in health, inflammation, disease progression and treatment response. It contributes to the Human Cell Atlas Immune Bionetwork and studies how circulating blood immune cells relate to cells in paired tissues. Translational projects focus on immune-related adverse events from immune-checkpoint inhibitor therapy, including checkpoint colitis and myocarditis, and on allergic asthma.

entries.name: Martin Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how human history shaped global genetic and phenotypic diversity. A main question is how well findings from Eurocentric genetic studies transfer to other ancestries. They develop and evaluate polygenic risk scores in multi-ancestry cohorts, including biobank and All of Us data, so that genetic prediction does not widen health disparities. They run psychiatric genetics case-control studies in African populations (for example NeuroGAP-Psychosis, with collaborators in eastern and southern Africa) and help train African researchers through the GINGER program. They also build community resources and statistical methods for diverse-ancestry data, such as the HGDP+1000 Genomes call set, and study fine-scale population structure and human evolution.

fit.reason: The lab does computational and statistical genomics, but on germline, population-level and polygenic work. It does not cover cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, somatic or structural variants, or single-cell and spatial omics, and a Canadian student would likely need a US visa.

entries.focus: The lab develops statistical methods for uncovering the genetic basis of human disease. It also studies the population genetics that underlie those methods. It centres on germline variation in human populations rather than tumour or somatic data.

entries.name: Klein Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how cells make fate decisions during development, tissue homeostasis and regeneration. It looks for quantitative rules and predictive models of how fate choice and tissue organisation work. It builds time-resolved single-cell maps of differentiation in several model systems, including a comparative angle on immune cell evolution in the tunicate Ciona. The methods are droplet microfluidics single-cell RNA-seq (inDrop), CAGE core-shell capsules for multi-step and live-cell single-cell assays, lineage tracing, imaging reporters, and computational inference of lineage-resolved trajectories and feedback.

fit.reason: The overlap is in single-cell methods and computational/statistical genomics tools, but the lab works on developmental and stem-cell fate rather than cancer, tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutations, so the fit is only partial.

entries.name: Segre Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and computational methods to find the causal genes, variants and regulatory mechanisms behind common eye diseases. These include primary open-angle glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and diabetic retinopathy. Methods combine GWAS with functional genomics (eQTL and splicing QTL mapping in human retina), single-cell data and systems biology, with the aim of interpreting noncoding variants. Current directions include drug repurposing for glaucoma and AMD, pharmacogenomics of ocular drug response, and non-negative matrix factorization to find biological subtypes of glaucoma. The PI also did earlier GTEx work and developed the MAGENTA pathway-enrichment method for GWAS.

fit.reason: The computational methods and single-cell/functional genomics work overlap with the student's methods interests, but the lab studies germline genetics of eye diseases, not cancer, tumour WGS/transcriptomes or somatic structural variants, and a US role would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Burge Lab
entries.focus: The lab's tagline is 'Computational Biology of Gene Expression'. It studies how RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) recognise RNA. This includes preferences for RNA structure, bipartite motifs and local sequence context. The main assay is RNA Bind-n-Seq (RBNS), which measures affinity across millions of RNA sequences for dozens of RBPs. The lab also builds quantitative biophysical and probabilistic models of RBP-RNA binding and of splicing, including alternative splicing and spliceosome behaviour, and it studies how splicing couples to transcription and gene expression (for example intron-mediated enhancement). Broader themes are microRNA regulation, human variation and disease, and the evolution of gene regulation. The work combines computational and experimental approaches.

entries.name: Robinson Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies genetic influences on behavior and cognition. It looks at neurodevelopmental variation and at differences within and between neuropsychiatric disorders, especially autism. Its methods come from statistical genetics and epidemiology, applied to common variants (GWAS meta-analysis, polygenic risk) and to rare variants. Current work extends the autism GWAS with new data from SPARK, the Autism Inpatient Collection and the NeuroDev project, and studies how common polygenic risk acts across brain cell types and tissues. The lab also works on psychiatric comorbidity in autism, such as anxiety and depression. Robinson co-chairs the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium Autism Working Group and the Broad's NeuroDevelopmental Variability Initiative.

fit.reason: The lab does statistical and population genetics of autism and psychiatric disorders, with little on cancer, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics. The only overlap is general computational genomics methods.

entries.name: Rheinbay Lab
entries.focus: The lab identifies and functionally characterizes non-coding cancer drivers in tumour whole-genome sequences. It develops new statistical and computational analysis methods and works with experimental collaborators to validate candidates. This builds on Rheinbay's 2020 Nature PCAWG/TCGA analysis of non-coding somatic drivers (point mutations and structural variants) in 2,658 cancer genomes. A second major theme is the role of the sex chromosomes in cancer, especially loss of the Y chromosome (LOY) in primary tumours. The lab also studies gender differences in cancer drivers, and has a Krantz award with Miguel Rivera on intrinsically disordered protein domains in cancer.

entries.name: Macosko Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops genomics technologies and uses them to study brain diseases, especially schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease. The methods build on Drop-seq, a single-cell RNA-seq method Macosko co-developed as a postdoc, and extend to Slide-seq and Slide-tags. These capture single-cell data at high spatial resolution in intact tissue. Other methods map synaptic connections and detect molecular interactions inside cells. Applications include identifying new brain cell types, studying how cells respond to psychological stress, and finding neurons vulnerable in neurodegenerative disease. The lab also builds cell atlases (braincelldata.org) and has a sizeable computational group.

entries.name: Lahav Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how single human cells turn signals into fate decisions such as growth, death, arrest and differentiation. They also ask why genetically identical cells respond differently. Most of the work is on the tumour suppressor p53, specifically how its dynamics after DNA damage determine cell fate, how p53 mutations change those dynamics, and how dynamics shape target-gene responses. Related projects cover DNA repair, cell growth and bHLH transcription-factor networks. Methods are live-cell fluorescence imaging of tagged proteins at single-cell resolution, quantitative image analysis, statistical analysis and mathematical modelling. The long-term goal is to use protein dynamics as a therapeutic target to steer healthy and cancer cells toward chosen outcomes.

fit.reason: The lab is cancer-relevant and single-cell, but it is wet-lab live-imaging and dynamical-systems work, with no focus on tumour WGS or transcriptome sequencing, structural variants, somatic mutation analysis or genomics ML. It overlaps only loosely with the student's single-cell interest.

entries.name: Hemberg Lab
entries.focus: The Hemberg Lab is a computational genomics group that develops machine learning and statistical methods for high-throughput single-cell data (transcriptome, epigenome, proteome and genome). Methods work includes spatial statistics to quantify cellular architecture in spatial transcriptomics, a faster and more scalable Harmony for batch correction and integration, and Scotia, which infers cell-cell ligand-receptor communication from spatial data. The lab also builds methods to detect tumour-derived RNA in blood from cell-free RNA sequencing for early cancer detection. Collaborations include pancreatic cancer spatial transcriptomics and proteomics (Hwang lab), CAR T-cell responses in solid tumours, influenza vaccine response, and perianal fistulizing disease.

fit.reason: The lab matches well on computational and ML methods and on single-cell and spatial omics in cancer, but it does little with tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation calling, and a US role would probably need a visa.

entries.focus: The lab studies how microbes evolve, with an emphasis on mobile genetic elements (plasmids, transposons and prophages) that replicate with their own evolutionary interests, which can conflict with those of their host cells. Methods combine synthetic experimental systems, large-scale computational analysis of clinical and environmental sequencing data, evolutionary theory, and technology development such as efficient microbial genome search.

entries.name: Springer Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how evolution shapes and constrains the way organisms respond to their environment. It compares cellular responses across related yeast species, using in vivo fluorescence, synthetic and genetic approaches, and numerical and analytical modeling. It also asks how biochemistry, molecular design and pathway wiring let cells process environmental information, using duplicated genes within and across species to study quantitative features of pathways. A current focus is cellular homeostasis, starting with pH homeostasis, including how protein overexpression affects total protein abundance and how much protein levels can vary before fitness costs appear.

entries.focus: The group works on statistics, data science and AI, and currently concentrates on statistical optimal transport and the mathematical foundations of Transformers. Its home page describes the span as 'from sequences to contacts to protein folding' and on to structures, networks, genomes and evolution. Methods are computational: coevolution and multiple-sequence-alignment analysis, protein language models, structure prediction and protein design. Recent papers cover what protein language models learn about coevolutionary statistics (PNAS 2024), stable de novo protein design (Nat Commun 2025) and stability prediction from mega-scale experiments (bioRxiv 2026). This is protein and evolutionary machine learning, not cancer or genomics-of-disease work.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational and machine-learning methods, but it works on protein structure and evolution, with no cancer genomics, structural variants, tumour sequencing or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.focus: The lab studies how genetic variation shapes human biology and disease, especially brain disorders such as schizophrenia and neurodegeneration. entries.name: Hovestadt Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies childhood brain tumors and leukemias, with a focus on pediatric brain tumors. It uses genome-wide DNA methylation profiling, analyzed with computational and machine learning methods, to classify tumor types, including rare ones. A methylation-based classifier developed by the lab is used in routine diagnostics. It also investigates non-mutational drivers, meaning epigenetic changes that switch on developmental genes in the wrong cellular context in tumors with few or no mutations in known cancer genes. Single-cell genomic techniques are used to study intratumor heterogeneity, subclonal evolution, cancer stem cell hierarchies, early tumorigenesis and therapy resistance.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with computational and ML methods for cancer genomics and with single-cell analysis of tumours, but the focus is pediatric brain tumour methylation and epigenetics rather than WGS, transcriptome or structural-variant analysis, and the role would need a US visa.

entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and machine learning methods for large-scale genetic, genomic and health data. Its best-known tools are STAAR, for rare-variant association testing in whole-genome sequencing studies, and FAVOR, a functional annotation resource for variants. Current work covers polygenic risk prediction, time-to-event analysis in WGS cohorts, causal mediation and causal inference, and predicting gene expression to link variants to phenotypes. Newer members work on generative modelling, optimal transport and manifold learning for single-cell and spatial multiomic data in the IGVF consortium. The lab is methods-focused and population-genetics oriented, and is not centred on cancer.

fit.reason: The lab overlaps on computational and ML methods for genomics and on single-cell/spatial omics (IGVF), but it does little cancer genomics, tumour sequencing or structural-variant work. It is also a US lab that would likely need a visa.

entries.name: Purdom Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical methods for high-throughput 'omics data, with a current emphasis on single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. A stated goal is to analyze a patient's whole single-cell profile, rather than individual cells, and link it to health outcomes so that outcomes can be predicted from single-cell data. Past lab work includes clustering of RNA-seq data, time-course gene expression analysis, and integration of multi-modal sequencing data. The work is methodological and statistical, not a wet-lab cancer genomics program.

fit.reason: Her single-cell and spatial omics methods and her statistical and machine-learning approach overlap with the student's computational interests, but the lab doesn't focus on cancer, tumour WGS, or structural variants, and it is a US lab (visa issue).

flags: No move: the PI is still at UC Berkeley Statistics, and her Biohub Investigator award (March 2022, five years) is an award, not a change of institution.

entries.name: Fox Group
entries.focus: The group develops Bayesian and probabilistic machine learning for complex time series. Methods include Bayesian dynamic modeling, sequence modeling and generative modeling, with an emphasis on interpretability and scalable computation. Applications cover machine learning for health (wearable sensors, health sensing), computational neuroscience (neuroimaging), and more recently multimodal biological data such as microscopy and omics. Her homepage describes the work as applying ML to health and biology. I did not find a specific cancer genomics program.

fit.reason: The group's ML methods and its recent omics and microscopy work are loosely relevant, but I found no cancer genomics, structural variant or somatic mutation work, and the focus is mainly health time series and neuroscience.

flags: I found no lab people page, so the PhD student list is empty. That is a gap in what I found, not evidence that she has no students. The lab homepage and the department profile list no students.

entries.name: AI and Computational Biology group (Biohub New York)
entries.focus: The group builds 'virtual cell models' of cellular dynamics and gene modules. It analyzes high-throughput omics, imaging and spatial data covering DNA, mRNA, enhancers, transcription factors, chromatin and proteins. It combines AI with statistical methods and prior scientific knowledge, and works closely with Biohub's experimental labs. One stated application is how enhancers govern immune responses in health and disease. Paull's background includes network inference and cancer-genomics methods (e.g. TieDIE, from his earlier work with Califano and Stuart).

fit.reason: The group does ML for genomics and single-cell/spatial omics, which matches the student's methods interests, but it focuses on virtual cells and immune enhancers rather than cancer WGS, structural variants or somatic mutations, and the roles are in the US (visa needed).

entries.name: Lareau Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression: how RNA sequence determines splicing, translation and protein output. It combines machine learning and computational modelling with high-throughput experiments to predict how sequence shapes the output of the genome. Current projects described in public member profiles include the effect of synonymous codon choice and slow codons on translation and protein output (yeast and human cells), and mRNA splicing, including engineering poison exons as a therapeutic strategy (a talk on Huntington's disease). The work centres on RNA biology and functional genomics, not cancer genomics.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational and ML methods for genomics, but its work is RNA regulation and translation, with no cancer, structural variant, WGS or single-cell/spatial focus.

entries.name: Barreiro Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how genetics and environment shape human immune responses, and why people and populations differ in susceptibility to infection and immune-related disease. It also studies how immune responses evolved in primates. Methods include population-scale transcriptomics and epigenomics, iPSC-derived macrophage systems, and single-cell RNA-seq. Examples are a rhesus macaque model of social stress and measurements of mRNA transcription rates during early infection, the latter with Yang Li under a CZ Biohub Chicago grant. Current NIH projects cover innate immune memory in humans and population variation in transcriptional responses to pathogens.

fit.reason: The lab shares the student's interest in computational transcriptomics and single-cell methods, but it studies immune and infection genetics, not cancer genomics, tumour whole-genome sequencing or structural variants. A US visa would also be needed.

entries.name: Altemose Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops new experimental and analytical tools to study how chromatin proteins regulate complex, repetitive regions of the human genome. A core method is DiMeLo-seq, which uses long-read, single-molecule DNA sequencing to map protein-DNA interactions and chromatin organization. Current projects include extending DiMeLo-seq to chromatin and gene regulation, and studying transcription factors that act on satellite DNA with microscopy, sequencing and biochemical labeling. The PI has a statistics/computational background (DPhil in statistics from Oxford), and the lab mixes wet-lab and computational work on centromeres and satellite repeats. This is not a cancer-focused lab.

fit.reason: The computational and sequencing-methods overlap is real, but the lab studies chromatin and repetitive-DNA biology in healthy genomes, with no focus on cancer, structural variants, somatic mutation or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.department_hint: EECS / Center for Computational Biology, UC Berkeley
entries.focus: The group develops computational methods to analyze and interpret personal genomes. A main thread is machine learning and deep learning to predict the clinical impact of genetic variation, including pathogenicity of missense and other variants; the PI previously co-developed the REVEL ensemble predictor. A second thread is deep learning models of sequence-to-function relationships, such as variation in gene expression and other molecular and cellular phenotypes. The EECS AI+Science page lists her interests as ML in genomics, variant effect prediction and sequence-to-phenotype prediction. The pages I could open did not mention cancer, somatic mutation or single-cell work.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with the student's interest in ML methods for genomics and some overlap with variant interpretation, but the group's focus is germline and personal-genome variant effects rather than cancer, structural variants, somatic mutation, or single-cell/spatial omics.

entries.name: Bateman Group
entries.focus: The group analyses protein sequences and structures to understand how proteins evolve and what they do. One main project is bacterial cell-surface proteins, especially fibrillar adhesins. These have a terminal adhesive domain on a stalk of repeated domains, and they matter for host colonisation, biofilm formation and vaccine design. The group studies them with AlphaFold structure prediction. A second project is spurious translated sequences in protein databases. The aim is tools that remove these contaminants from sequence sets. The wider team also runs the UniProt, InterPro and RNAcentral resources.

fit.reason: The work is protein sequence and structure bioinformatics, with essentially no cancer genomics, structural variants, somatic mutation or single-cell/spatial omics, so it overlaps only in general computational methods.

entries.name: Cortes-Ciriano Group
entries.focus: The group develops computational tools for cancer genomics. One theme is genomic instability and immune escape: how complex chromosomal alterations drive cancer and affect immunotherapy response, including analysis of long-read sequencing data. A second theme is early cancer detection, using multi-omic liquid biopsy methods based on nanopore sequencing, including minimal residual disease monitoring. A third theme is single-cell genomics, covering clonal evolution, the timing of somatic mutations and their fitness effects. The group also analyses somatic mutations in sequencing data, and the PI received an ERC Consolidator Grant in December 2025 on genome structure and gene regulation in disease.

fit.reason: Very strong overlap with the student's interests in cancer WGS, structural variants and somatic mutation analysis, computational methods, and single-cell cancer genomics, but the lab is UK-based, so a visa would likely be needed.

flags: PI is still at EMBL-EBI. A December 2025 EACR piece and the 2025 EMBL-EBI research review list him there, and I found no sign of a move.

entries.focus: The lab applies evolutionary principles to predict the trajectory of individual cancers, with an emphasis on metastasis and drug resistance. It is a multidisciplinary team of cancer geneticists, computational biologists and clinician scientists. Main programmes are clear cell renal cell carcinoma (conserved evolutionary trajectories, patient-derived organoids, tumour immune response) and melanoma (evolution under therapy resistance). Featured projects include TRACERx Renal (nongenetic evolution in ccRCC), a whole-genome sequencing study of ccRCC, the MANIFEST immunotherapy biomarker platform, and a diet/obesity and kidney cancer collaboration with the Crick and MD Anderson.

entries.name: O'Connor Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical and mathematical methods to characterize the genetic architecture of common diseases and complex traits. One thread quantifies how common and rare variants contribute to disease and how natural selection shapes that architecture. Current projects include integrating functional annotations, characterizing the genetic architecture of autism, and forecasting rare-variant association study results at larger sample sizes. A second thread builds genealogy-based representations of linkage disequilibrium and genotype data, which speed up LD-matrix computations and heritability partitioning. The work is population/statistical genetics (GWAS and rare-variant analysis) and not tumour sequencing.

fit.reason: The lab does computational and statistical methods development for genomics, which overlaps with the student's methods interest, but it works on germline GWAS and rare-variant genetics and not on cancer, tumour WGS or transcriptomes, structural or somatic variants, or single-cell and spatial omics.

entries.name: Keating Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies how proteins interact in eukaryotic signaling and how those interactions affect human health. It combines computational modeling with experiments to work out how amino acid sequence controls binding specificity. It then designs peptides and other molecules that selectively disrupt particular interactions. A current focus is the Bcl-2 family of apoptosis regulators, where structure-based and machine-learning models of BH3-motif helix binding have produced selective peptide reagents for profiling apoptosis in cancer cells. The lab is also expanding into TRAF and EVH1 domains that bind short linear motifs. Methods include machine learning for protein and peptide design, structural modeling, yeast surface display, and biophysical and structural assays.

fit.reason: The lab does protein and peptide design and structural biochemistry, so it has almost no overlap with cancer genomics, structural variants, sequencing analysis, or single-cell and spatial omics. The only link is the use of machine learning and an apoptosis-in-cancer application.

entries.name: Bryson Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and the host macrophage response. It builds tools and models that span scales, from single infected cells to whole animals, and draws on both immunology and microbiology. Two central questions drive the work. The first is which macrophage processes kill bacteria effectively, and how the bacteria resist that stress. The second is how macrophage plasticity can be manipulated to control macrophage function. The long-term goal is to modulate macrophage function and inform TB vaccine design. The group uses experimental and computational approaches, including single-cell methods, but its focus is infectious disease and immunology, not cancer.

entries.name: Greener Group (biomolecular simulation / force fields)
entries.focus: The group works to make molecular dynamics simulations more accurate for biology. Current force fields can fail on disordered proteins and protein aggregation. One approach trains faster molecular mechanics force fields with graph neural networks, using quantum mechanics and experimental data. The aim is a reproducible method that works across all biomolecules. A second approach builds fast machine learning interatomic potentials for biomolecular systems, using simpler models and GPU programming, with the long-term goal of simulating enzyme reactions. The group also works on differentiable simulation (the Molly.jl package in Julia), protein design with simulation, protein folding and free-energy methods.

fit.reason: The group does ML-driven biomolecular simulation and force-field development, with no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variant or single-cell/spatial omics work, so it overlaps with the student only through general computational and ML methods.

entries.focus: The lab studies functional genetic variation in human populations. entries.department_hint: Computer Science / Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics
entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods, based on statistics, machine learning and efficient algorithms, for high-throughput functional genomics. These are mainly multi-modal single-cell, spatial and genome-editing technologies, and the lab applies them in immunology and cancer. One thread characterizes CD8 T cell states and the regulation of T cell activation, using single-cell and spatial multi-omics, including Tcf7 regulators in tumour CD8 T cells. A second thread studies how Foxp3 and related factors shape chromatin organization and gene expression in regulatory T cells. A third thread builds CRISPR guide-RNA design tools (GuideScan and GuideScan2), including for noncoding regions and batch screens. Other published methods include ArchVelo (trajectory modeling), Gloss (cell-cell interactions) and a benchmark of spatial transcriptomics deconvolution.

entries.name: Kennedy Lab
entries.focus: The lab uses mathematical modeling and model-informed data analysis to study how the organization of nervous systems relates to their function. It focuses on brain circuits for fear, survival and social behavior, including the hypothalamus (social and defensive behavior), the basal ganglia (behavior selection) and the hippocampus (social-bond formation). Methods include dynamical systems, control theory, reinforcement learning, statistical modeling and machine learning. Current projects include reservoir computing and spiking networks with heterogeneous cell types, and machine-learning models for forecasting and analyzing animal behavior. The work is computational and theoretical, not genomic.

fit.reason: The lab does theoretical and computational neuroscience of behavior and neural dynamics. It has no cancer genomics, sequencing, structural variant or single-cell omics work. The only overlap is the general use of machine learning, and a US visa would likely be needed.

entries.focus: The lab develops computational methods for structure-based drug discovery and applies them to therapeutically relevant targets. entries.name: Lundberg Lab
entries.focus: The lab studies human cell biology through spatial proteomics. It combines bioimaging, mass-spectrometry proteomics and AI to map where proteins sit within cells, how those locations change over time, and how mislocalization contributes to disease. The long-term goal is a spatiotemporal proteome model of a human cell, built by applying machine learning to imaging data integrated with other data types, with the aim of improving drug discovery. The lab creates the subcellular section of the Human Protein Atlas (Cell Atlas). Current work includes multiplexed immunofluorescence, Deep Visual Proteomics, generative and foundation models of microscopy images, 'digital twin' cell models, and cilia biology. The lab also supports open science and runs crowd-sourced challenges.

fit.reason: The lab has strong ML and some spatial-omics overlap, and a few members work on tissue or early-cancer imaging. It does not do cancer genomics, WGS/transcriptome sequencing or structural-variant analysis, so it is a weak match for this student's core interests. The student may also need a US visa.

entries.name: Palacios Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops Bayesian nonparametric and probabilistic models for evolutionary and population-genetic data. Its methods include new coalescent models, Gaussian-process priors for effective population size trajectories, and efficient MCMC and other computational-statistics tools. Much of the work is on phylodynamics and inference of phylogenetic tree distributions for infectious disease, including ranked tree shapes and reporting delays in real-time analyses. The lab also works on single-cell lineage tracing, and its stated applications include genetics, health and cancer.

fit.reason: The lab is a methods-focused statistical phylogenetics group. Its overlap with the student's interests is limited to computational/ML methods and single-cell lineage tracing, and it does not work on tumour WGS, structural variants or somatic mutation calling.

entries.name: Salzman Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops statistical algorithms that run inference directly on raw sequencing data, without relying on reference genomes or annotations. Its main tool is SPLASH (and the related NOMAD), a reference-free framework that finds sample-dependent sequence variation in DNA or RNA-seq. It has been applied to alternative splicing, RNA editing, V(D)J recombination, viral and microbial diversity, and non-model organisms. Cancer-related work includes gene fusion discovery and validation, splice-site analysis, circular RNA detection in single-cell RNA-seq, and statistics for spatial transcriptomics (e.g. MERFISH). The long-term aim is unified models of genome evolution, regulation and function.

fit.reason: Strong match on computational and statistical methods for transcriptome data, including fusions, single-cell and spatial omics; it is only partly cancer-focused, has little somatic-variant or WGS work, and is a US lab that would need a visa.

entries.name: Steinmetz Lab
entries.focus: The lab develops experimental approaches to read, edit and write whole genomes, with the long-term goal of assigning a function to every nucleotide in the human genome. Its quantitative genetics work uses functional genomics and genome-editing screens (CRISPR-Cas9 and multiplexed editing) to study how genetic variants and environment shape complex traits. Its precision health work studies disease mechanisms in yeast, mouse and human models, including patient-derived cells, with examples such as dilated cardiomyopathy and ME/CFS. It also builds genomics technologies, including single-cell RNA-seq and multi-omics methods, and contributes to synthetic genome work (Sc2.0). Current projects include combinatorial perturbations with machine learning and mapping lifespan-regulating pathways.

fit.reason: The lab shares an interest in single-cell/multi-omics methods and some machine learning (Bezney's project), but it is mostly wet-lab functional genomics in yeast and human cell lines, and I found no cancer genomics, tumour WGS or structural variant analysis. It also needs a US visa.

entries.focus: The lab does population-scale genetic analysis, combining genomic and phenotypic data from very large biobanks. It builds statistical models and computational tools for this, including fast penalized-regression methods and genome-wide association studies. Methods include mechanistic and dynamical modeling, systems biology, and machine learning for cell phenotype prediction.

They also study cellular responses to stress, such as reactive oxygen species, the unfolded protein response and DNA-damage memory involving p21. They also build quantitative image-analysis and visualisation tools such as PhenoPlot, and use machine learning for 3D cell-shape profiling.

entries.name: Andrés Group (population/evolutionary genomics), UCL Genetics Institute
entries.focus: The group studies how populations evolve and adapt to their environment, using modern and ancient genomes to detect natural selection. It works mainly on humans and endangered primates. A major theme is selection that maintains diversity within populations (balancing selection) or creates differences between populations. Other topics are adaptive introgression, sexually antagonistic variation and mito-nuclear co-evolution. Methods are population-genetic and statistical, such as ancestral recombination graphs (ARGs), selection scans, and experimental evolution in Drosophila.

fit.reason: The group does computational genomics and method development, but it is evolutionary and population genetics with no cancer, tumour sequencing, structural-variant, somatic-mutation or single-cell work, so only the general computational-methods interest overlaps.

entries.focus: The group combines machine learning with high-throughput biochemistry, such as peptide-display screening of kinases. Disease focus includes brain tumours such as glioblastoma, and leukaemia.

It develops interpretable deep-learning models of cell structure and function, and network-based biomarkers for patient subtypes and treatment response. It created Cytoscape, the network analysis software. Larger programs include the NCI Cancer Cell Map Initiative, Bridge2AI Cell Maps for AI (CM4AI), and the ARPA-H ADAPT Dynamic Digital Tumors project for precision oncology. The lab has also worked on epigenetic aging clocks.

fit.reason: The lab's cancer network, machine-learning and tumour-modelling work overlaps with the student's interest in computational methods for cancer. It has little focus on whole-genome sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics, and a move would need a US or UK visa.

entries.name: Sebé-Pedrós Group
entries.focus: The lab studies how cell type programs and their genome regulation evolve. It uses comparative regulatory genomics across animals and unicellular eukaryotes. Its methods include single-cell transcriptomics, scATAC-seq and chromatin profiling, 3D genome organization, and lineage tracing. It also coordinates the Biodiversity Cell Atlas, which aims to map cell types across the tree of life, and works on biodiversity epigenomics, meaning the evolution of chromatin, transcription factors and histone modifications. The work is evolutionary biology and basic regulatory genomics. It does not study cancer or disease.

fit.reason: Single-cell omics and computational analysis overlap with the student's methods interests, but the lab works on evolution in non-model organisms, with no cancer, structural variant or somatic mutation work, and the main base is in Spain, not the UK.

entries.name: Lehner Group
entries.focus: The group combines large-scale DNA mutagenesis experiments (deep mutational scanning), genomics, biophysics, mechanistic modelling and AI to learn how sequence changes alter proteins and RNAs. Topics include protein stability, allostery, sequence-to-affinity and selectivity, amyloid aggregation, RNA splicing, stop codons, and protein evolution and engineering. The goal is predictive and programmable molecular biology, with machine-learning models trained on massive experimental datasets. Current projects include enzyme and transcription-factor allostery, intrinsically disordered regions, and de novo antibody design.

fit.reason: The group is strong in ML for genomics and variant-effect prediction, but it works on protein and RNA biophysics with no cancer genomics, tumour sequencing, structural variants or single-cell/spatial omics. A UK role would also need a visa.

entries.focus: The lab combines mathematical models, pathogen genomic data and large-scale human mobility data (mobile phone and satellite data) to study how infectious diseases spread and how to control them. entries.focus: The group develops mathematical and statistical tools that connect pathogen genome sequences to infection ecology, evolution and public health. Main topics are phylogenetic tree methods (tree space, comparing and summarising trees, BEAST2 and time-tree distributions) and phylodynamic inference of transmission from genomic data. They also work on multi-pathogen interactions, co-infection and the evolution of antimicrobial resistance (e.g. S. pneumoniae and M. tuberculosis). entries.name: Lee-Six Group
entries.focus: The group studies how somatic mutations interact with cell state and tissue context to decide which cells outcompete their neighbours. It focuses on the earliest stages of paediatric disease, especially childhood cancers. Its aim is to work out how mutation identity, cell state and the surrounding tissue environment determine whether a mutant cell becomes a tumour. Methods combine mutation detection (laser capture microdissection and duplex sequencing) with spatial transcriptomics on human paediatric tumour and normal tissue, plus quantitative modelling and in vitro testing, including iPSC genetic manipulation.

fit.reason: Strong overlap with somatic mutation analysis, cancer genomics and spatial omics, but the focus is paediatric and normal-tissue clonal dynamics rather than tumour WGS and structural variants, and the group is in the UK, so a visa would be needed.

entries.focus: The group explores human brain cellular diversity using large-scale approaches. entries.name: Meta FAIR
entries.focus: FAIR Chemistry builds open datasets and machine-learning models for molecules and materials. It grew out of the Open Catalyst Project. Its OMol25 dataset, built with Berkeley Lab, has over 100 million DFT-calculated 3D molecular snapshots of up to 350 atoms. It covers most of the periodic table, with biomolecules, electrolytes and metal complexes as the three main focus areas. Alongside it, FAIR released the Universal Model for Atoms (UMA), an equivariant graph neural network. UMA is trained on more than 500M DFT calculations and is meant to work out of the box as an atomistic simulation model. The work is molecular and atomistic (chemistry, catalysis, materials, biomolecular interactions). I found no genomics, sequencing or cancer-biology programme on this team.

fit.reason: The team does atomistic and quantum-chemistry ML. It has no overlap with cancer genomics, structural variants, tumour sequencing or single-cell/spatial omics, apart from general ML-methods skills.

entries.name: Amazon / AWS
entries.focus: AWS Healthcare AI and Life Sciences builds cloud and AI products for drug discovery and healthcare. Its flagship, Amazon Bio Discovery, launched in April 2026. It is an agentic application for early-stage drug design, focused on antibodies. It gives researchers a catalog of biological foundation models from partners such as Apheris and Boltz, with a benchmark dataset to compare them. A natural-language AI agent helps design experiments, pick models and choose candidates. Models can be fine-tuned privately on an organisation's own lab data. Candidates go to integrated lab partners (Twist Bioscience, Ginkgo Bioworks) for synthesis and testing, and the results feed the next design cycle. Early adopters include MSK, Bayer, the Broad Institute and Voyager Therapeutics. Amazon's research effort on genomics and oncology data is not documented in what I found.
